title: Authentication versus authorization (who you are vs what you can do)
hook: Authentication answers who is calling your API. Authorization answers whether that caller may perform the action. Mixing them up leads to wrong HTTP status codes, security holes, and failed interviews.

blocks.text: Authentication (AuthN) verifies identity — proving the caller is who they claim to be (username/password, JSON Web Token (JWT), API key, certificate). Authorization (AuthZ) decides permissions after identity is known — can this user read orders, delete tenants, or call admin endpoints? In ASP.NET Core, UseAuthentication populates HttpContext.User; UseAuthorization evaluates [Authorize] attributes and policies against that principal.

entries.plainDefinition: Process of verifying identity and building a ClaimsPrincipal on HttpContext.User.
entries.example: JwtBearerHandler validates signature and sets User

entries.plainDefinition: Process of checking whether the authenticated principal may access a resource or perform an action.
Represents the authenticated user with a collection of claims (name, role, tenant id).
No identity established — User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated is false.

blocks.text: Every protected Web API endpoint runs through both stages. Returning 403 Forbidden when the client sent no token (should be 401 Unauthorized) breaks API clients and OAuth flows. Skipping authorization because authentication succeeded assumes all authenticated users have equal access — a common breach pattern. Senior interviews expect you to explain status codes, middleware order, and when to fail closed.

blocks.title: Fail closed
blocks.body: Default protected endpoints should reject unknown identity (401) and known-but-unauthorized identity (403). Never fall through to business logic without an explicit [AllowAnonymous] or public endpoint.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Request flow through AuthN then AuthZ

items.title: Routing selects endpoint
items.body: Endpoint routing attaches [Authorize] metadata to the matched route before auth middleware runs.

items.title: Authentication middleware
items.body: UseAuthentication invokes registered handlers (JWT Bearer, cookies). On success, HttpContext.User is set. On failure or missing credentials, User may remain anonymous — handler does not always short-circuit.

items.title: Authorization middleware
items.body: UseAuthorization checks endpoint metadata. If [Authorize] requires auth and User is not authenticated → 401. If authenticated but policy fails → 403.

items.title: Endpoint executes
items.body: Handler runs only if authorization succeeded. Additional resource-level checks (ownership) may still return 403 inside the action.

diagram.title: Authentication vs authorization in the pipeline
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  REQ[HTTP Request] --> RT[Routing\nendpoint metadata]
  RT --> AUTHN[UseAuthentication\nwho are you?]
  AUTHN --> AUTHZ[UseAuthorization\nwhat may you do?]
  AUTHZ -->|401 no identity| R401[401 Unauthorized]
  AUTHZ -->|403 identity ok policy fail| R403[403 Forbidden]
  AUTHZ -->|allowed| EP[Endpoint handler]

snippet.label: Register AuthN and AuthZ in Program.cs
snippet.explanation: AddAuthentication registers handlers; AddAuthorization registers policies. Middleware order: routing, then authentication, then authorization, then endpoints.

snippet.label: 401 vs 403 on a controller
snippet.explanation: [Authorize] without policy only requires authentication (401 if missing). Policy failure after authentication yields 403. [AllowAnonymous] opts out of fallback policy.

snippet.label: Resource-level authorization inside the action
snippet.explanation: Middleware authorization is coarse (endpoint + policy). Fine-grained ownership checks belong in the handler and still return 403 Forbid(), not 401.

snippet.label: Diagnostic — log AuthN vs AuthZ outcome
snippet.explanation: Production triage: 401 usually means fix client credentials or token validation. 403 means identity is valid but claims or ownership failed.

blocks.title: AuthN vs AuthZ in Express/NestJS vs ASP.NET Core
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Returning 403 when no token was sent (should be 401). Checking roles only in the controller without [Authorize] on the endpoint. Calling UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication. Assuming JWT presence means authorization — validation and policies are separate steps.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: Application Insights dependency tracking on JWT metadata refresh failures correlates with 401 spikes. Custom metrics on 401 vs 403 ratio — sudden 403 increase often means policy or claims mapping regression after identity provider change. OpenTelemetry spans on JwtBearerHandler.OnAuthenticationFailed show signature vs expiry vs audience failures separately from authorization policy denials.

blocks.title: JWT session vs server session (AuthN tradeoffs)
rows: Cannot revoke instantly without blocklist or short TTL + refresh
Sticky sessions, server store (Redis), harder for pure APIs
Extra latency per request to identity server
Long-lived secret — rotation and scoped keys critical

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying authentication and authorization are the same thing. Returning 403 for missing Bearer token. Not knowing UseAuthentication does not block anonymous requests by itself — [Authorize] and authorization middleware do. Claiming JWT replaces authorization entirely.

interviewTakeaways: Authentication = identity (who); authorization = permission (what) — separate middleware and HTTP status codes.
401 when identity missing or invalid; 403 when identity valid but policy or ownership fails.
Production tip: alert on 401/403 ratio shifts; log IsAuthenticated on 403 to distinguish policy bugs from token issues.

60s: AuthN sets HttpContext.User via UseAuthentication. AuthZ runs after and returns 401 without identity, 403 when policy fails. JWT proves identity, not permission — policies and handlers enforce AuthZ.
Follow-up: how do refresh tokens fit if access JWT is stateless?
commonPitfalls: Saying '403 for expired token' gets you rejected — expired JWT fails authentication (401), not authorization.
Only checking User.IsInRole in code without [Authorize] — endpoint may be reachable if routing misconfigured.
Strong answer: '401 means no valid principal. 403 means principal exists but policy or resource check failed. I use fallback policy plus explicit AllowAnonymous on public routes.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: passport.authenticate establishes req.user (AuthN); a separate role check middleware is AuthZ — same two-step split as UseAuthentication then UseAuthorization.
JwtAuthGuard mirrors authentication middleware; RolesGuard or custom PolicyGuard mirrors IAuthorizationHandler — guards run after identity is attached.
